HyperFrames renders HTML to video by seeking a paused timeline frame by frame, so every render is identical; the person edits the same files in the Studio preview. ## Contract

`npx hyperframes check --json` reports most violations with a `Fix:` line.

1. Every timed element has `class="clip"`, `data-start` and `data-duration` in seconds, and shows over `[start, start + duration)`: land an end state just before its end. `data-track-index` is only a Studio lane; paint order is `z-index`.
2. The video's length is the root's `data-duration`: overrun is cut, an early end holds the last frame.
3. Each composition builds one paused timeline and registers it after its tweens: `window.__timelines["<data-composition-id>"] = tl`.

5. Never tween `display`, `visibility` or `autoAlpha` on a `.clip`; animate a child.
6. No CSS `transform` on an element GSAP transforms; animate transforms, not `left`/`top`/`width`/`height`.
7. Never `play()`, `pause()` or seek media. A `<video>` keeps its sound with `data-has-audio="true"`, else it is `muted`; music, voice, replacement sound and J/L cuts are a separate `<audio>`.
8. Every `<audio>` has an `id` or it is left out of the mix. No `crossorigin` on media. Time a `<video>` or its wrapper, never both.
9. Only the bundled fonts (`references/format.md`) resolve by name; any other family needs `@font-face` to a file in `assets/fonts/`.
10. Asset paths are root-relative (`assets/...`), in sub-compositions too.

12. A scene file puts its styles, markup and scripts inside `<template>` and styles its root as `#root`. Intended overflow or overlap: `data-layout-allow-overflow`, `data-layout-allow-overlap`.

# Music videos and films cut to a track

The song is the structure. Timing facts (hits, beat trust, loops) are in `../film.md` "On music"; this file is the shape.

## Song structure becomes edit structure

- Find the sections first: `npx hyperframes audio <track> --only sections,onsets,moments --json`. Each section is a chapter: intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro.
- Cut density follows energy: slower shots in verses, one picture per strong beat in the chorus, a held image on a breakdown.
- The chorus returns to one home stage and escalates each time it comes back; the ending rhymes with the opening.
- Chapter breaks land on section boundaries, with a transition that belongs to the film's medium (a brush wipe, a paper tear, a match cut).

## Pictures for the words

- Each lyric line or phrase gets its own picture (shots of about 1.4–4 s): show what the line means, not the line itself. Lyrics on screen only when asked; then each line holds at least a beat and is set as type, not subtitles.
- Something happens in every shot, and every cut has a cause on screen.
- A song about something real gets real material (footage, photos, places); an abstract track gets one world with a strong medium.

## The look

A physical medium carries a music film further than effects: watercolour with ink outlines, cut paper, risograph print, film grain on footage. Characters, if any, act (`character.md`).

## Tells for this type

The same treatment for more than about 6 s; a spectrum bar or waveform as the main picture; every cut on every beat; words about the music rather than the song's own world.

# Motion

## Motion craft

Measured frame by frame from the official HyperFrames launch films. These are defaults: a reference the person gave, or a Moment that does otherwise on purpose, wins for its own beat.

- **Moves**: a fast move takes 0.3–0.6 s and carries motion blur on its own ease, peaking at its fastest frame: 6–12 px on text-sized elements, 15–20 px full-frame, horizontal-only on a horizontal move. One move is one tween.
- **Arrive slow, leave clean**: long-tailed ease-outs on arrivals; landing takes longer than leaving. An exit is one smooth motion, never slide, stop, then leave. Entrances that are too snappy read as glitches; slowing the whole video by about a second often fixes it.
- **Ease by role**: an arrival lands on a long tail (`expo.out`, `power4.out`), a camera move or a colour flood eases both ways (`power2.inOut`), a zoom through or an exit accelerates (`power3.in`). The same `power2.out` at 0.5 s on everything is the flat default that makes a film feel generated. Linear only for rotation, progress and constant speed that is the point.
- **Springs** are named by damping ratio: 1.0 never bounces, 0.7-0.85 reads premium, 0.4-0.6 playful, under 0.3 a cartoon. Position and size may bounce; opacity and colour never do. GSAP's `elastic.out(1, 0.5)` and `back.out(1.4)` are the nearest built-ins; a closed-form spring of `t` keeps any frame renderable on its own.
- **Exits** are 40-50% shorter than their entrances. **Overlap**: the next element starts when the previous is 30-50% done; fully sequential looks robotic, all at once looks cheap. **Stagger**: letters a frame apart, words 60-120 ms, list items 40-80 ms.
- **Beat grid**: frames per beat = fps × 60 / BPM; compute each beat from its index and round it, never add a rounded beat repeatedly (at 128 BPM and 30 fps that drifts 2 frames in 32 beats). Cut on the beat, change the layout on the bar.
- **Cuts**: cut at the fastest frame of a move, with matching direction and speed on both sides. A click into a new screen is a match cut on the click's rebound; the new screen comes in slightly large and settles.
- **Titles**: a landed title is dead still; the motion moves to the next element, the camera or the world behind. Vary the entrance within a film, never a fade and slide-up for each:
  - per word: `blur(6px)` → 0 and opacity 0 → 1 in 0.13 s, 0.067 s apart, no translate;
  - per word from light grey to ink, 0.07–0.1 s apart, no position change;
  - the whole line blurring in, 8 px → 0 in 0.13–0.2 s;
  - per letter for a name, 0.1 s apart, opacity 0.3 → 1 with a slight blur;
  - behind the subject: the title between the plate and a matte of the person;
  - one word of the sentence rolling through options like a slot machine, about 0.1 s a roll.
- **Holds**: a line the viewer must read holds about 0.5 s plus 0.3 s a word, the film's last line at least 2 s; a one- or two-word chapter line may hold 0.4 s. Then exit with a blur-out and fade of 0.13–0.25 s, word by word, or with the scene's move.
- **Title size**: 4–9% of the frame height, one or two lines; quiet lines at 2.5–4% against hero words that fill 60–90% of the width. One highlighted word in the accent colour, which carries meaning.

# Animation runtimes

HyperFrames seeks each frame on its own, so motion must be a function of time, never of the previous frame. Full GSAP reference: `npx hyperframes docs gsap`.

## GSAP facts that bite

- Register the timeline last. Building inside `document.fonts.ready.then(…)` or another async callback is fine if you register at the end of it; registering first renders blank (`gsap_timeline_registered_before_async_build`).
- Place tweens at absolute seconds (`tl.to(el, {…}, 2.4)`). Set start states in the tween (`fromTo`), not in CSS.
- Measure layout once before building tweens, never inside `onUpdate`.
- Finite repeats only: `repeat: Math.max(0, Math.floor(duration / cycle) - 1)`.
- Seed randomness with a small PRNG (mulberry32).
- A scene's timeline can't reach elements outside its file, and two timelines must not animate the same property of one element.
- Transforms on a `<span>` need `display: inline-block` or `block`.
- Text that must fit a width: `window.__hyperframes.fitTextFontSize(text, { fontFamily, fontWeight, maxWidth })` returns `{ fontSize }`; `window.__hyperframes.pretext` measures text without a reflow.

## Other runtimes

| Runtime                      | Use for                           | How HyperFrames drives it                                                                        |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| CSS `@keyframes`             | Simple loops and decoration       | Found automatically; finite iterations, `animation-fill-mode: both`, `data-start` on the element |
| WAAPI                        | Native keyframes                  | `element.animate(…, { fill: "both" })` then `pause()`; times are document time, so use `delay`   |
| Lottie / dotLottie           | After Effects exports, characters | `autoplay: false`, always set `loop`, push the instance to `window.__hfLottie`                   |
| anime.js v4                  | Existing anime code               | `autoplay: false`, push to `window.__hfAnime`, `anime.createSeededRandom`                        |
| Three.js, WebGPU, p5, canvas | 3D and generative                 | Draw from `e.detail.time` in an `hf-seek` listener; set `data-duration` on the root              |

Charts and map overlays: drive them from a GSAP tween's `onUpdate`, not the library's own transitions. A real place is shown on baked imagery, not drawn (`film.md` "Maps and real places"). Heavy setup (big meshes, shader compiles) registers a `window.__hf.buildReady["<key>"]` promise.

## The seek protocol

```html
<script>
  function renderAt(t) {
    /* draw the frame for t seconds from state derived from t alone */
  }
  window.addEventListener("hf-seek", (e) => {
    renderAt(e.detail.time);
    // async work (GPU submit, image decode): e.detail.waitUntil(promise), called synchronously
  });
  renderAt(0);
</script>
```

No `requestAnimationFrame` loop or timer as the clock.

When handing a project back to the user, use the Studio project URL, not the source `index.html` path:

```text

```

Use the actual port and project directory name; treat `index.html` as source-code context, not the preview surface. For example, after `npx hyperframes preview --background --port 3017` in `codex-openai-video`, report `http://localhost:3017/#project/codex-openai-video`.

`preview --context` and `preview --selection` are the agent bridge into a running Studio session. They do **not** start a new server; they find the active preview server for the current project, read agent-useful state from Studio, print it, and exit.

Use it when the user gives deictic edit instructions like "change this", "move the selected element", "make the card I clicked bigger", or "fix the current selection":

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection
```

The compact context payload includes the selected element's source file, composition path, current timeline time, `data-hf-id` / selector target, bounding box, text content, and a thumbnail URL for the selected element. Prefer `selection.target.hfId` when present; fall back to `selection.target.selector` only when no stable `data-hf-id` exists. ```bash

npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields lint
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection,lint
```

Use `--context-detail full` only when the edit genuinely needs heavy selection fields such as `computedStyles`, `inlineStyles`, `dataAttributes`, or editable text-field metadata:

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection --context-detail full
```

`preview --selection --json` remains available when you explicitly want the full selected-element payload and do not need lint/server context.

| Code                       | Meaning                                                                    |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `preview-not-running`      | Start Studio first with `npx hyperframes preview --background`.            |
| `ambiguous-preview-server` | Multiple matching Studio servers are open; rerun with one listed `--port`. |
| `preview-port-mismatch`    | The requested `--port` is not one of the matching Studio servers.          |
| `no-selection`             | Studio is open, but the user has not selected an element yet.              |
| `selection-unavailable`    | The running preview server does not expose selection context cleanly.      |

```bash

`play` serves the composition through the embeddable `<hyperframes-player>` web component instead of the full Studio UI. Use it when sharing a preview link or when Studio is heavier than needed (no editor, no panels). `play` reports the plain `http://localhost:<port>` URL — no `#project/<name>` fragment (that's a Studio routing convention only `preview` uses).

The player's `playback-rate` attribute (preview speed control, drives the timeline's `timeScale`) is clamped to `[0.1, 5]`; values `≤ 0` or non-finite fall back to `1`. This is a preview/playback knob, not a composition `data-*` attribute — authored motion still renders at `1×`.

Both `preview` and `play` can open inside an explicit Chromium-compatible browser instead of the OS default. Two use cases: isolated Chromium profile, or external CDP attach (DevTools / Playwright / Puppeteer / browser-MCP). **HyperFrames itself does not own CDP automation** — this only exposes the endpoint; whatever connects to it is your problem.
